File:Abrosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Abrosaurus is a basal macronarian sauropod dinosaur known from an exceptionally well preserved skull. Like all sauropods, it was a quadrupedal herbivore with a long neck. It had a boxy head, a typical trait of macronarians, topped with a bony arch that supported the nostrils. Abrosaurus was small by sauropod standards, at just 9 m in total body length.

File:Athenar TD.png.ImageDescription: Athenar is a dicraeosaurid sauropod from the Morrison Formation of North America. This formation preserves many different sauropods, exhibiting niche partitioning - similar animals adapting to different survival strategies. Dicraeosaurids like Athenar browsed low vegetation, thereby avoiding competition with higher-reaching sauropods.

File:Atlasaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Atlasaurus is a brachiosaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic period of what is now Morocco. A basal member of the brachiosauridae, Atlasaurus had the longer forelimbs typical of this group, but a proportionately larger head, shorter neck, and longer tail. Atlasaurus is estimated at around 15 m in length, and weighed around 23 t.

Although a very early and unspecialized sauropod, Barapasaurus shows the building plan typical for later, more derived sauropods: a long neck, short trunk, and columnar limbs which indicate an obligate quadrupedal posture

File:Brachytrachelopan TD.png.ImageDescription: Brachytrachelopan is a dicraeosaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic of what is now Argentina. Dicraeosaurids are typically small in terms of sauropods, and Brachytrachelopan was no exception. It grew to about 10 m in length, and weighed around 5 t. Brachytrachelopan is notable for having the shortest neck in proportion to body size of any sauropod. This is likely because it was adapted to fill a certain niche, feeding on vegetation around 1-2 m in height.

File:Campananeyen TD.png.ImageDescription: Campananeyen is a rebbachisaurid sauropod that lived approximately 100 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous of what is now Argentina. Rebbachisaurids are the main group of diplodocoidea to have lived past the Jurassic, and had a more horizontal posture than contemporary sauropods, mainly the titanosaurs. They are unique among sauropods for having batteries of teeth used for chewing, rather than the typical peglike teeth sauropods used to strip leaves off branches.

File:Chucarosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Chucarosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Argentina, known from fairly intact remains of the left limbs, including a 1.9 m femur. It was a large, slender-limbed colossosaur - 25 m in length, and weighing around 30 t. Characteristics in its hips, forelimbs, and hindlimbs suggest that despite its massive size, Chucarosaurus was slender and more gracile than would be otherwise expected for such a large animal.

File:Cienciargentina TD.png.ImageDescription: Rebbachisaurids are the latest known sauropod dinosaurs outside the titanosaur lineage. Cienciargentina is a rebbachisaurid from the Late Cretaceous, making it among the most recent. It had many hollow bones, and likely had batteries of teeth used for chewing, a rebbachisaurid feature unique among sauropods.

It was around 28m long. The neck was unusually deep, and the backbone supported a wide rib cage.

File:Gandititan TD.png.ImageDescription: Gandititan is a basal titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now China. It was a long-necked herbivore, typical of sauropods, with a relatively short tail, a characteristic of titanosaurs compared to other sauropods. Titanosauria have a wide range of body sizes, and Gandititan falls around the middle, slightly on the smaller side. Discovered with a fairly well articluated spine from neck to tail, Gandititan is estimated at about 14 m in total body length.

File:Jiangxititan UDL.png.ImageDescription: Jiangxititan a titanosaurian sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of China. Typical for a sauropod, it had a long neck and stood on four pillar-like legs to support its massive body. Jiangxititan is a member of the Lognkosauria, which include some of the largest dinosaurs known, and is one of the few from mainland Asia. The discovery of Jiangxititan demonstrates the presence of both early-diverging and late-diverging titanosauriform sauropods in that area during the Late Cretaceous.

File:Jinchuanloong TD.png.ImageDescription: Jinchuanloong is a relatively basal sauropod that measured an estimated 10 m in length. Sauropod skulls typically don't preserve well in the fossil record, but Jinchuanloong is known mainly from the skull, and parts of the neck and tail. Like all sauropods, Jinchuanloong was a quadrupedal herbivore that used its long neck to reach the vegetation that it fed on.

File:Jingiella TD.png.ImageDescription: Jingiella is a mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Dongxing Formation of Guangxi, China. The name honors people of the Jing Nationality. Mamenchisaurids are known not only for being generally large dinosaurs, but for their necks being among the longest in proportion to body-length, even compared to other sauropods. Like all sauropods, Jingiella walked on four pillar-like legs and subsisted on a herbivorous diet.

File:Lingwulong TD.png.ImageDescription: Lingwulong is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Yanan Formation in China. It is the earliest-aged neosauropod ever discovered, as well as the only definite diplodocoid from east Asia. Unique traits that distinguish Lingwulong from other diplodocoids include highly elaborated ornamentation along the upper margin of the orbital area and anterior dorsal vertebrae. File:Lishulong TD.png.ImageDescription: Lishulong is a basal sauropodomorph from the Early Jurassic. Typical of the sauropodomorphs of that time, Lishulong was a bipedal herbivore with a proportionately small head atop a long neck. Its teeth and neck suggest it likely fed on both ground-level and mid-height vegetation. Lishulong measured around 11 m in length, and weighed about 3 t.

File:Massospondylus TD.png.ImageDescription: Massospondylus carinatus is a mid-size basal sauropodomorph dinosaur, reaching approximately 4 m in length, and weighing 1 t. Like most early sauropodomorphs, it had a slender body, long neck, and proportionally small head. Massospondylus is generally thought to be herbivorous, but it may have been omnivorous.

File:Mesetasaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Mesetasaurus is a titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Uruguay. Like all sauropods, it stood on four pillar-like legs, using its long neck to reach the vegetation it fed on, counterbalanced by its long tail. Relatively small for a titanosaur, Mesetasaurus grew to approximately 10 m in length.

File:Musankwa TD.png.ImageDescription: Musankwa is a basal sauropodomorph from the Late Triassic of what is now Zimbabwe. The early sauropodomorphs, or prosauropods, were likely omnivorous, as they represent an evolutionary transition between early theropods and the large herbivorous theropods. Like many other prosauropods, Musankwa was likely an obligate biped, walking only on two legs. It grew to about 4 m in length, and weighed upwards of 400 kg.

File:Mussaurus patagonicus.jpg.ImageDescription: Life restoration of a juvenile Mussaurus patagonicus eating a Dicroidium fern. Mussaurus (mouse lizard) was named for the diminutive size of the holotype specimen, now known to represent a juvenile individual. File:Nagatitan TD.png.ImageDescription: Nagatitan is the largest known dinosaur from Southeast Asia, at approximately 27 m in length, and weighing around 27 t in total body mass. As a sauropod, it was a quadrupedal herbivore, using its long neck to reach vegetation, which it processed in its large gut. The discovery of Nagatitan has expanded known titanosauriform diversity within the region.

File:Nigersaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Nigersaurus is a sauropod dinosaur known for having over 500 teeth, all of which were situated at the front of its strangely shaped snout. File:Petrustitan TD.png.ImageDescription: Petrustitan is titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from what is now Romania. It showed evolutionary affinities to South American titanosaurs, strengthening the hypothesis that these sauropods spread north during the Early Cretaceous. Petrustitan was much smaller than its southern counterparts, a result of adapting to life on the European archipelago.

File:Phosphatotitan TD.png.ImageDescription: Phosphatotitan is a titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from what is now Morocco. It is most closely related to South American titanosaurs, indicating Late Cretaceous titanosaur diversity in the Southern Hemisphere may be underestimated. Smaller than its South American counterparts, Phosphatotitan is estimated at around 4 t in total body mass.

File:Titanomachya TD.png.ImageDescription: Titanomachya is a titanosaurian sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of what is now South America. The name alludes to the battle in which the mythological Greek Titans were defeated, as a reference to being near the extinction of the titanosaurs. Like all sauropods, Titanomachya was herbivorous and stood on four legs, with a long neck and tail. However, it is extremely small for a titanosaur, at only 6 m in length, and weighing about 8 t in body mass.

File:Tongnanlong TD.png.ImageDescription: Tongnanlong is a large mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur that lived in the Late Jurassic period of what is now China. Typical of mamenchisaurids, it had an extremely long neck, even by sauropod standards. Tongnanlong grew to approximately 25 m in length and weighed 20-30 t, making it one of the largest mamenchisaurids.

File:Udelartitan TD.png.ImageDescription: Udelartitan is a titanosaurian sauropod from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Uruguay. It had the typical sauropod body plan, standing on four thick pillar-like legs, and possessing a long neck. Titanosaurs are a very diverse group, Udelartitan was a small one, estimated at only 15 m in body length. Though a skull has yet to be discovered, it probably had peglike teeth, and a large gut for processing vegetation.

File:Uragasaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Uragasaurus is a sauropod dinosaur, and the first mamenchisaurid known from Thailand. Mamenchisaurids exhibit the basic sauropod body plan, processing their herbivorous diet in their large gut. Uniquely, mamenchisaurid necks, like that of Uragasaurus, are proportionately long, even by sauropod standards.

File:Uriash TD.png.ImageDescription: Uriash is a European titanosaur with evolutionary affinities to those from the southern continent of Gondwana. Its discovery strengthened the hypothesis that titanosaurs spread from the south in the Early Cretaceous. Small for a titanosaur, Uriash is one of the largest known from the European archipelago at about 10 m in length, and weighing 5-8 t in body mass.

File:Yeneen TD.png.ImageDescription: Yeneen is a relatively small titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina. Like all sauropods, it stood on four pillar-like legs, and used its long neck to reach vegetation. As a saltasauroid titanosaur, Yeneen likely had rows of osteoderms down its back.
